newsitem.title: LEBANON: Arabs must strengthen primary capital markets.
newsitem.headline: Arabs must strengthen primary capital markets.

text.p: Arab countries must strengthen their primary capital markets, create market makers, introduce new financial instruments and open up to foreign investors, Arab financiers said on Thursday.

Speaking on the second day of the Third Arab Capital Markets conference held in Beirut, prominent Saudi financier Saleh Abdallah Kamel of Dallah al-Baraka group said the success of primary markets determined the success of Arab capital markets.

"One of the negative impacts of the little attention paid to primary markets is the adoption of the turnover criteria as the main and only criteria when determining the efficiency of Arab financial markets," Kamel told 400 financiers and economists.
"The Arab market is still limited. It lacks depth and is secluded rather than open to non-national investors," he added.
He said the measurement of efficiency of any financial Arab market should be based on its ability to absorb and accumulate savings before directly investing them in development-oriented projects.

"Total capitalisation of the Arab market has not exceeded $108 billion by the end of December 1996 which is small compared to the $760 billion of financial assets owned by the Arab private sector and invested in international markets," he added.
Speculation by investors hunting for easy cash should be restricted because Arab capital markets, unlike western markets, are incapable of absorbing its effects.
"Widespread speculation in our Arab markets leads to turning away real investors and savers from entering markets, which transforms our financial markets into gambling clubs," he added.
Kamel cited various examples of discrepancy in book and market values of various stocks saying the complete separation between these two values resulted from speculation.
He said interest in primary markets should come through the creation of new companies, transformation of family companies into corporations, and the enlargement of privatisation processes.

He pointed that the average rate of active investors in Arab financial markets against total adult population was two percent against 37 percent in the United States, saying it was an indication of little investor confidence in these markets.

Securities Manager at the British Bank of the Middle East in Jordan Ziad al-Basha said some one million Jordanian citizens out of a population of four million were involved in the Amman stock exchange activity.
"It is a success story. It tells you that people have confidence in the economy," he told Reuters.
Some 98 companies, mostly industrial, are listed on the Amman exchange where 27 licensed brokerage firms operate. Capitalisation of the markets is $5 billion.
Basha said inital public offerings totalled $1.4 billion in Jordan over the past three years, more than in the previous 20 years.

Ahmed el-Helw, Managing Director of Cairo finance house Intercapital Securities said the government of Egypt has kept is promises to open up the country to foreign investors and to implement privatisation.
Last week, the government decided to privatise 40 percent of Misr for Aluminium -- a step to be followed by privatisation of the rest of the country's heavy industries.
"This year, the government has partially privatised 10-12 public companies through initial public offerings ranging between 10 and 30 percent," he said.

"On top of that, the government has dropped regulations that differentiated between foreign investors and Egyptians. It has established rules aimed at rather encouraging foreign investors to come into the market," Helw said.
The Amman Stock Exchange regulations allow foreign investors to own up to 50 percent of the capital of any listed firm. The Tunisian exchange puts the limit at 49 percent.
Morrocco provides no such restrictions while Lebanon imposes them on real estate companies.
Gulf markets are mainly restricted to Gulf investors. Investment by non-Gulf Arabs and foreigners is mostly restricted to mutual investment funds.
